Graded trustworthy; Ahmad bin Hanbal called him truthful, reliable and established with all his teachers, and Ibn Hibban, Abu 'Awana and al-Hakim included his narrations in their collections. He was the maternal brother of Musawir al-Warraq, and sources note confusion between him and another narrator called Sayyar Abu Hamza.

bio: Grandson of both Hasan ibn Ali and Husayn ibn Ali. His sons Muhammad, Ibrahim and Idris led rebellions against Abbasid rule, and Idris established the Idrisid dynasty in Morocco. He was imprisoned by al-Mansur for refusing to reveal his sons' hiding place and died in al-Hashimiyya prison near Kufa in 762, and is considered a martyr among Shi'as.
research_evidence: Some sources mention that Abd Allah was assassinated on the orders of al-Mansur in al-Hashimiyya prison, near Kufa in 762.

bio: Son of the famous companion Abdullah ibn Salam; the Prophet seated him in his lap and named him. Scholars disagreed on his status: Ibn Abi Hatim said he only saw the Prophet without companionship, while al-Bukhari credited him with companionship. Ibn Sa'd called him trustworthy with sound narrations; he transmitted a hadith about the Prophet eating barley bread with dates. He died during the caliphate of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz.
research_evidence: Died during the caliphate of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz (no specific AH year stated). Identified as the young companion Yusuf ibn Abdullah ibn Salam; our record likewise has no death year.
dod_s: c. 680 CE (estimated from generation — no recorded date survives)

He was unanimously rated trustworthy (thiqa) by Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Yahya ibn Ma'in, Abu Zur'a, al-Ijli, Ibn Hibban and Ibn Hajar, and Ibn Hibban included him among the reliable narrators of the Successor generation. The page places his death between 131 and 140 AH without a precise year.

bio: Shurahbil ibn Sa'd, Abu Sa'd al-Madani, was exceptionally knowledgeable about the participants of Badr and the Prophet's military expeditions (maghazi). His reliability was contested: Yahya ibn Ma'in authenticated him in one report and weakened him in another, and Ibn Hajar classed him as truthful but confused toward the end of his life. Malik ibn Anas refrained from narrating directly from him, concealing his name in transmissions.
research_evidence: Death year 123 AH (approximately 741 CE).

full_name_ar: عبد الرحمن بن عسيلة أبو عبد الله الصنابح
city: Medina, then Damascus (settled in the Levant)
bio: A Yemeni who migrated intending to meet the Prophet but arrived too late — he was at al-Juhfa when the Prophet died five nights earlier, making him a mukhadram whose reports from the Prophet are mursal. He narrated from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and Bilal, settled in the Levant, and was considered reliable (thiqa) by Ibn Hajar and others, though sparse in hadith transmission.
classif: mukhadram (met the Companions, not the Prophet)
research_evidence: Died after 70 AH, during the caliphate of Abd al-Malik (no precise year stated); our record likewise has no death year. Full name عبد الرحمن بن عسيلة, kunya Abu Abdullah, and mukhadram/early-Successor status match our record.
dod_s: c. 714 CE (estimated from generation — no recorded date survives)

Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Yahya ibn Ma'in, al-Ijli and al-Nasa'i all declared him trustworthy. Sufyan ibn Uyayna said of him 'your eyes have not seen his like' and ranked his memorization of Tawus's transmissions above that of Tawus's own son.

bio: Hajjaj ibn Abi Uthman al-Sawwaf, a sixth-generation Basran narrator and mawla of al-Taw'ama bint Umayya ibn Khalaf, earned his living as a cloth merchant. Ahmad ibn Hanbal, Ibn Ma'in, Abu Zur'a, Abu Hatim, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i all declared him thiqa, and Yahya al-Qattan described him as intelligent, accurate and shrewd. Ibn al-Madini ranked him among the three most reliable transmitters from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir, alongside al-Awza'i and Husayn al-Mu'allim.
research_evidence: Death year reported variously: "135هـ، أو 143هـ، أو 144هـ" (135 AH, or 143 AH, or 144 AH); Ibn Shahin noted one report of 144 AH.

bio: A companion who settled in Jerusalem (Bayt al-Maqdis) and died there at age 75; sources differ on the year (58, 64, or 41 AH). Appointed governor of Homs by the caliph 'Umar, he was the nephew-relation of the poet Hassan ibn Thabit's family, and Abu al-Darda' said of him: 'the jurist of this community is Shaddad ibn Aws.' He was renowned for devotion, praying restlessly through the night, and about 50 hadiths are attributed to him.
research_evidence: توفي ٦٤ هـ; the page also records the alternative reported death years 41 AH and 58 AH. He died in Jerusalem at age 75.

He was regarded as wise and generous; his name derived from a foot affliction. He initially supported Ali but later aligned with Mu'awiya, and declined to aid al-Husayn despite a direct request.

Ibn Hajar rated him trustworthy except in his narrations from 'Ikrima, which critics found anomalous, and he was accused of Kharijite views. Malik transmitted from him and defended his honesty, saying such men 'would sooner fall from heaven to earth than tell a lie.'

He was the uncle of Muhammad ibn Sulayman.

bio: A Kufan narrator of the sixth generation, of the Banu Dabba, nephew of the jurist 'Abdullah ibn Shubruma — sources note he was regarded as superior to his uncle. Rated trustworthy (thiqa) by Ibn Hajar, Ibn Ma'in, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Sa'd and Ya'qub al-Fasawi, with Abu Hatim calling him 'sound in hadith'. He had roughly thirty hadiths; some of his transmissions from Ibn Mas'ud were judged mursal (discontinued).
research_evidence: Death year: 140 AH (stated in source); sixth generation (الطبقة السادسة), Kufan (الكوفي)

He was rated thiqa (reliable) by Yahya ibn Ma'in and Abu Dawud, and Ibn Hibban listed him in al-Thiqat. He transmitted from Successors such as Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and the judge Shurayh, and Sufyan al-Thawri and Shu'ba narrated from him.

Abu 'Awana and al-Darimi included his narrations in their collections.

bio: A Basran narrator of the sixth tier, great-grandson of the Companion Anas bin Malik and father of the judge Muhammad bin 'Abdullah al-Ansari. Scholarly opinion on him was mixed: Ibn Hajar summarized him as 'truthful but with many errors' (صدوق كثير الغلط), al-Daraqutni and al-'Ijli considered him trustworthy, while al-Nasa'i called him 'not strong' and Ibn Ma'in dismissed him. Abu Hatim noted he did not meet Anas directly.
research_evidence: Died between 171-180 AH (exact year not definitively stated); sixth tier (الطبقة السادسة), Basran, kunya Abu al-Muthanna
dod_s: c. 753 CE (estimated from generation — no recorded date survives)

Ibn Sa'd placed his death at the start of the caliphate of Abu Ja'far al-Mansur.
research_evidence: Death year: 142 AH; Ibn Sa'd: 'He died at the beginning of Abu Ja'far's caliphate'

bio: Malik ibn Dinar was a Basran tabi'i, preacher and Qur'an teacher regarded as a reliable traditionist in Sunni sources. He is credited with formulating an early Sufi concept of 'inner jihad' — fighting one's desires as one fights enemies. He showed appreciation for Christian teachings and may have studied the New Testament; South Indian tradition also links him to the spread of Islam in Kerala.
research_evidence: He died just before the epidemic of plague which caused considerable ravages in Basra in 748-49 CE (traditions place death at 744-45 or 747-48 CE)

bio: A Damascene narrator of the ninth generation, client (mawla) of Ramla bint 'Uthman, and a Hanafi jurist noted for Murji'i theological leanings. Ibn Hajar rated him 'trustworthy, though accused of irja'', and Ibn Ma'in, al-Nasa'i, Duhaym and Ibn Hibban confirmed his reliability. bio: A prominent early Muslim of Damascus, counted among the Eight Ascetics, whose real name is given as Abdullah ibn Thawb. He is famed for being thrown into a fire in Yemen by the false prophet al-Aswad al-Ansi for refusing to acknowledge him, and emerging unharmed; Umar likened his experience to that of Abraham. He died during an expedition against the Byzantines in the reign of Muawiya II.
research_evidence: Died: 684 CE

Al-Dhahabi called him trustworthy and Ibn Hajar saduq; Waki' counted him among the people's memorizers though confused in two narrations. His grandson Muhammad ibn Ayyub compiled Fada'il al-Qur'an.

bio: Yahya ibn al-Mutawakkil, Abu 'Aqil al-Madani (also said al-Kufi), an eighth-generation transmitter who settled and died in Baghdad, known as the companion of Bahiyya. Critics condemned him almost uniformly as weak (Ibn Hajar, al-Nasa'i: da'if; al-Dhahabi: 'they weakened him'); Ahmad ibn Hanbal deemed his reports from Bahiyya on Aisha's authority reprehensible and unique to him.
classif: Mawla of the family of Umar
research_evidence: هـ 167 (died 167 AH, in Baghdad)

He reportedly buried his written notes and then narrated from memory, multiplying his errors; Ibn Hajar called him saduq with bad memory, al-Daraqutni reliable but frequently erring, and al-Bukhari said munkar al-hadith.

bio: Eldest son of the caliph Abu Bakr; four consecutive generations of his direct male line were Companions of Muhammad. He initially fought on the Quraysh side at Badr and Uhud, converting to Islam after the Treaty of Hudaybiyya in 628, and later distinguished himself as a champion swordsman of the Mubarizun, reportedly killing several Byzantine champions in single combat at Yarmouk. He opposed Yazid I's appointment, withdrew from Medina to Mecca, and died at al-Habshi near Mecca, being buried in the Mala cemetery.
research_evidence: In 675 CE (53 AH or 55 AH), following his staunch opposition to the appointment of Yazid I, Abd al-Rahman left Medina for Mecca to seek sanctuary in the Haram. (675 CE is within 2 years of our recorded 677 CE.)

bio: A Medinan transmitter, ally (halif) of Banu Adi ibn Ka'b, whose father Amir ibn Rabi'a fought at Badr. Born in the Prophet's lifetime but only about four or five at his death, scholars disagreed whether he heard from the Prophet directly; he is classed among the senior Successors and transmitted mainly from the Companions. His kunya was Abu Muhammad.
research_evidence: 70 هـ، أو 85 هـ، أو 89 هـ (died 70, or 85, or 89 AH; al-Tirmidhi's reference specifies سنة تسع وثمانين, 89 AH). The 85 AH report matches our record.

bio: Maymun ibn Abi Shabib, Abu Nasr, a third-generation Kufan (also said to be of Raqqa) who worked as a merchant. He narrated frequently with disconnected (mursal) chains, including reports from Abu Dharr and Mu'adh ibn Jabal. Ibn Hajar called him saduq with much irsal, al-Dhahabi a truthful merchant, Abu Hatim sound in hadith, while Ibn Ma'in graded him weak.
